plain: The 14 research documents this site was built from, read as one body.
The list of 100 individual findings pulled out of those documents, each recorded with what it says and how well it is supported.
Counting a study once even when several reports cite it, so shared literature is not mistaken for independent agreement.
Pushing back against a message because it feels like an order. Measured as a small but consistent effect across many studies.
The quick judgement a reader makes about what a message means for him, before he decides how to feel about it.
The reason a message works, stated as a step: which need it meets or which cost it removes. Not a guarantee that it works.
A study that pools the results of many earlier studies to estimate an overall effect. Usually stronger evidence than any single study.
A test where people are randomly given one version or another, which is the only design that can show one wording caused a difference.
How big a difference something makes, separate from whether the difference is real. A real effect can still be small.
A test that varies two or more things at once so their separate and combined effects can be told apart.
How explicitly a message says it is about men, from not at all, through simply naming the audience, to defining what a man should be.
The circumstances under which a finding stops holding. Naming one is how two apparently opposed findings turn out to be compatible.
A ranking from 1 to 5 where the order is meaningful but the gaps are not measured. A move from 1 to 2 is not necessarily the same size as 4 to 5.
What a study actually counted. Attitudes, intentions and behaviour are different outcomes, and a message can move one without moving the others.
Whether a finding is about men in particular or about people in general who happen to have been studied as men.
A structured way of combining qualitative studies to build an explanation rather than to count results. Abbreviated CIS.
The proportion of a message made up of moral words, as opposed to how much moral weight it carries in total. The two behave differently.
How well supported a claim is, on this site's own scale from strong down to weak, plus two off-scale labels for observed practice and cross-report inference.
